title: AUAO v1.0 Graph Relationship Specification
description: Formal edge relationship definitions for the AegisSwarm Universal Attack Ontology (AUAO v1.0) graph representation.

relationship_types.name: USES
relationship_types.description: Indicates that an attack technique employs a specific obfuscation, encoding, or sub-technique.

relationship_types.name: TARGETS
relationship_types.description: Specifies the architecture component, guardrail, or model element aimed at by the attack.

relationship_types.name: CAUSES
relationship_types.description: Relates an attack technique directly to its primary security consequence or impact.

relationship_types.name: ESCALATES_TO
relationship_types.description: Denotes privilege escalation or transition from a low-severity vector to a critical control compromise.

relationship_types.name: REQUIRES
relationship_types.description: Specifies pre-conditions, agent capabilities, or context windows needed for the attack to succeed.

relationship_types.name: BYPASSES
relationship_types.description: Identifies the specific defense mechanism, alignment, or content filter evaded by the technique.

relationship_types.name: LEADS_TO
relationship_types.description: Defines multi-stage attack chains where one successful exploit unlocks subsequent execution phases.

relationship_types.name: MITIGATED_BY
relationship_types.description: Maps the recommended security control, guardrail, or architecture pattern that neutralizes the attack.

relationship_types.name: OBSERVED_IN
relationship_types.description: Links the attack class to public research datasets, red team benchmarks, or real-world CVE disclosures.

relationship_types.name: SIMILAR_TO
relationship_types.description: Establishes semantic equivalence or tactical similarity between attack methodologies.

relationship_types.name: DEPENDS_ON
relationship_types.description: Indicates tactical prerequisite dependencies between multi-turn or multi-stage payloads.

graph_edges.description: Direct system prompt override explicitly bypasses initial prompt framing.
System prompt subversion frequently leads directly to full system prompt leakage.
PDF indirect injection often uses zero-width or hidden text encodings.
Indirect document injections often attempt downstream tool command execution.
DOM element injection targets automated web browsing agents.
Gradient-computed adversarial suffixes disrupt token refusal boundaries.
Crescendo attacks share multi-turn gradual drift dynamics with Socratic safety bypass.
Command line parameter injection can escalate to full Python REPL sandbox breakouts.
Unauthorized tool invocation bypasses manual approval confirmation prompts.
Spoofing an MCP server allows hijacking tool calls and exfiltrating data.
Poisoned MCP prompt resources subvert the client-side system prompt assembly.
Document poisoning corrupts vector database search outputs.
Adversarial embedding collisions target high cosine similarity matches.
Long-term memory injection permanently alters agent behavior across session resets.
Cascading multi-agent propagation leads to multi-agent consensus poisoning.
Sandbox escape provides arbitrary read/write access to host file systems.
Visual prompt injection conceals attack text within image pixel channels.
Base64 encoding evades static keyword safety classifiers.
